title: Strong quantum IOPs with polynomial communication
formal: Does every QMA promise problem have a strong quantum interactive oracle proof with polynomial communication, constantly many messages and a constant total number of queried message qubits? More precisely, for every \(L\in\mathrm{QMA}\), do there exist a polynomial \(p\), constants \(r,q\in\mathbb N\), and one uniform verifier under the strong access rules below such that, on every input \(x\) of length \(n\), its running time and total incoming prover-message length are at most \(p(n)\), the total number of messages is at most \(r\), the total query cost is at most \(q\), and \[x\in L_{\mathrm{yes}}\Rightarrow\sup_P\Pr[V_x\leftrightarrow P\text{ accepts}]\ge2/3,\] \[x\in L_{\mathrm{no}}\Rightarrow\sup_P\Pr[V_x\leftrightarrow P\text{ accepts}]\le1/3?\] Here \(P\) ranges over all allowed prover strategies, with no computational bound. Strong means that the verifier returns each incoming quantum register in full and sends no additional quantum register of its own.
why: This asks whether very local interactive verification of quantum evidence can avoid enormous communication while obeying the strong return rules. Resolving it would clarify the joint limits of proof length, local access and interaction for QMA.

progress.text: The source proves polynomial communication in the general model and exponential communication in the strong model, both with constant query and message bounds; Question1.9 asks for polynomial communication in the strong model.

The later construction achieves polynomial communication with polylogarithmic queries and rounds in a model retaining parts of the initial witness. These bounds do not settle the stated strong constant-query question.

context_blocks.text: An interactive oracle proof distinguishes the amount of information transmitted from the amount inspected. A verifier may receive a long register while touching only a few of its qubits. The question requires a polynomial bound on the first resource and a constant bound on the second, together with a constant number of interactions.

The source distinguishes general, restricted and strong access models. Strong protocols return the whole incoming quantum register and send no additional verifier-generated quantum register. These restrictions still allow private workspace. The existing exponential-communication construction happens to operate on constantly many total qubits, but that stronger property is not built into formal Definition5.13.

The source obtains polynomial communication and constantly many queries in its general model. That construction distributes verifier-generated entanglement, which the strong rules forbid. Its separate strong construction uses exponentially many communicated qubits. Question1.9 asks whether polynomial communication can be obtained in the strong model.

The June2026 paper obtains polynomial communication with polylogarithmically many queries and interaction rounds. Its description also retains an initial prover witness and returns successive blocks across rounds, rather than returning the entire incoming register each turn. These parameters and access rules do not establish the selected constant-query, constant-message strong statement.

The June paper discusses conditional improvements from quantum codes with stronger parameters. Such a conditional parameter discussion is not an unconditional construction satisfying all the present access and resource requirements. The card therefore retains the original open question.

A quantum proof need not remain unchanged after inspection, and the prover may keep entanglement across the interaction. Consequently, soundness concerns the complete sequence of allowed strategies, rather than independent checks of fixed classical strings.

definitions:
A promise problem \(L=(L_{\mathrm{yes}},L_{\mathrm{no}})\) is a pair of disjoint subsets of finite binary strings; inputs outside these sets have no correctness requirement. QMA is the class of such pairs with a uniform polynomial-time quantum verifier receiving one polynomial-size quantum witness. For every yes-input there is a witness accepted with probability at least \(2/3\); on a no-input every witness is accepted with probability at most \(1/3\). Uniform means that a single deterministic classical algorithm generates the input-dependent circuit in polynomial time. Its private ancillas start in zero. Gate count, number of qubits and witness length are polynomial in the classical input length. The witness can be any density matrix and need not be efficiently preparable.

A qubit has state space \(\mathbb C^2\). A density matrix is Hermitian, positive semidefinite and of trace one: \(\rho=\rho^\dagger\), \(v^\dagger\rho v\ge0\) for all vectors \(v\), and \(\operatorname{Tr}\rho=1\). A quantum channel is a complex-linear map on matrices that preserves trace and remains positive when tensored with the identity on an arbitrary auxiliary register. Verifier operations are uniformly described polynomial-size circuits of fixed elementary gates, zero-state preparations and computational-basis measurements with classical control. For a concrete universal gate convention take \[H=2^{-1/2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix},\quad T=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&e^{i\pi/4}\end{pmatrix},\quad\mathrm{CNOT}|b,c\rangle=|b,b\oplus c\rangle.\] Here \(b,c\in\{0,1\}\), \(\oplus\) means addition modulo two, and \(i^2=-1\). No arbitrary numerical matrix is a free gate. Channel descriptions include their finite circuit realization; all uniform classical computation and elementary gate operations count toward running time.

An interactive proof has one verifier and one prover, exchanging a bounded sequence of registers and classical messages. They begin with no shared entanglement. The verifier has private workspace \(R\) initialized in zero, containing both its quantum memory and classical records. The prover has an unrestricted private register and may apply any quantum channel to its own memory and the messages it receives; its strategy can depend on \(x\) and the prior interaction. It may entangle different messages with its private memory and with returned registers. Soundness must hold against every such strategy, even computationally unbounded ones. The honest prover is also allowed to be unbounded, as in the source's formal Definitions5.14–5.15. Neither efficient preparation of an honest quantum witness nor a bound on the honest prover's computation is part of this question.

In one verifier turn, let the incoming prover register be \(W=(W_1,\ldots,W_\ell)\). It can contain quantum data or classical data encoded in the computational basis; reading a bit in such a message is still a query. The verifier first applies a channel only to its private register \(R\), then measures an address register in \(R\) to obtain a classical list specifying a set \(S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,\ell\}\) of at most \(q_i\) positions. Conditioned on these addresses, it applies a circuit channel only to \(R\) and the qubits \(W_S\). Its operation is identity on the other incoming wires. This is the query-channel structure of Definitions5.1–5.2: the addresses may depend on private randomness and earlier rounds, but are classical measurement outcomes before the current message is touched. Coherent querying in a superposition of addresses, or choosing a second set adaptively after inspecting the same message within this turn, is not this one-batch query operation. Repeated local gate operations on the already selected qubits affect running time but do not add new positions to that turn's query set.

After its turn the verifier returns the entire \(W\) register to the prover and retains only its own private register. It may also send polynomially many classical bits, but no additional quantum register. The returned qubits may have changed through the allowed interaction; their original state need not be restored. Keeping information acquired in private workspace is allowed, including quantum information transferred through the queried-qubit channel. The restriction forbids keeping incoming message wires between turns, not all changes to private memory. The verifier's own quantum workspace may be polynomial: the formal strong model does not impose a constant bound on all its private qubits. Merely forwarding the unqueried wires counts as communication, but is not counted as inspecting them. At its final turn the verifier produces an accept/reject bit, returning the message if a return is needed to respect the same convention; a final unused return changes the constant message bound only by one.

The incoming message lengths \(\ell_i\), the query budgets \(q_i\), and the protocol's uniform circuit descriptions are fixed by the input and protocol; branchwise budgets may be bounded by fixed worst-case values. Total prover-message length is \(\sum_i\ell_i\), including every incoming copy or retransmission of a register. Total query cost is \(\sum_iq_i\), counting access again if a position is queried in a later message. All resource bounds hold on every branch, not only in expectation or for the honest prover. Returning the full registers adds at most the same quantum communication again. Classical messages generated by the polynomial-time verifier are also polynomially bounded. The constants \(r,q\), the polynomial \(p\) and the verifier may depend on the promise problem but not on \(n\) or the individual input. A polynomial bound on communication does not permit polynomially many queried qubits: the latter must remain a constant.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the stated inclusion of QMA in the constant-message, constant-query strong class with polynomial communication, or a complete Lean-checked proof that some QMA promise problem admits no such verifier. An affirmative construction must prove uniform resource bounds, completeness and soundness against arbitrary entangled adaptive prover strategies. A negative result must quantify over all eligible verifiers and all constants and polynomials in the definition. Exponential communication, polylogarithmic queries or messages, retaining part of an incoming register between rounds, or sending extra verifier-generated quantum registers does not meet the target. No computational hardness assumption can replace the required unconditional soundness. A protocol with constant private quantum space would suffice, but that extra condition is not necessary in the selected formal model. This is an exact class-inclusion question, not a numerical approximation target.

importance.reason: Tests how far succinct interactive verification can extend to quantum proofs with explicit communication restrictions; affects a broad proof-system design space.

sentences: Interactive oracle proofs let a verifier inspect only selected parts of much larger prover messages.
This question asks for constant-round quantum versions that verify all QMA promise problems with polynomial total communication and only constantly many queries.
The strong quantum access model is part of the target, because different ways of querying quantum messages permit different verification strategies.
Soundness must cover arbitrary prover behavior, while the verifier remains efficient and has a constant completeness-soundness gap.
The project probes how far proof compression and local checking can extend when the evidence itself is quantum.
